decks.title: Unseen Passages — Part 1: The Discursive Passage
goals: Use a five-step plan to read any unseen passage efficiently
Skim for the main idea and scan for details
Identify a writer's claim, reasons, counter-point and conclusion
Make inferences and name a writer's tone with evidence
Work out word meanings from context and answer 1-mark and 2-mark questions

slides.heading: Unseen Passages — Part 1: The Discursive Passage
slides.body_md: CBSE Class 10 English, **Section A: Reading Skills (20 marks)**. Two unseen passages, ten marks each. This part teaches the discursive passage; Part 2 teaches the case-based factual passage with a visual.

rows: Discursive passage: a writer discusses an issue, argues a view or weighs both sides
Case-based factual passage with visual input (table, chart or similar)

visual.alt: Table of the two Section A questions: question one, a discursive passage of four hundred to four hundred and fifty words for ten marks; question two, a case-based factual passage with a table or chart, two hundred to two hundred and fifty words, for ten marks.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section A: Reading Skills, 20 marks.

slides.narration: Welcome to reading skills. Section A of your English paper has two passages you have never seen before. The first is a discursive passage of about four hundred words, where a writer discusses an issue or argues a view. The second is a shorter factual passage with a table or chart. Each is worth ten marks, so this section alone is a quarter of the paper.

slides.heading: What is a discursive passage?
bullets: It **discusses** an issue: the writer has a view and tries to convince you.
It gives **reasons and examples**, and often admits the other side.
Topics are everyday and wide: habits, environment, technology, education, society.
Questions test the **argument**, not your knowledge of the topic.
slides.narration: A discursive passage discusses an issue. The writer has a point of view, gives reasons and examples, and often admits a limit or the other side before concluding. The topic could be anything from screen time to city trees. Remember that every question is about what this writer says and how they say it, not about what you already know on the subject.

slides.heading: A five-step plan for any passage
slides.body_md: Reading the questions first tells you **what to look for**, so your first reading is already purposeful.

visual.alt: Flow of the five-step reading plan: read the questions, skim for the gist, scan for each answer, read those lines closely, then answer and check.
visual.caption: SOYL five-step plan for any unseen passage.

slides.narration: Here is a plan that works for every passage. First, read the questions, so you know what to look for. Second, skim the passage for its main idea. Third, scan for the part of the passage that answers each question. Fourth, read those lines closely. Fifth, write your answers and check them. With practice this whole cycle takes about twenty minutes per passage.

slides.heading: Skimming and scanning

rows: title, first and last paragraphs, first line of each paragraph
very fast, jumping to the target
who, when, how many, which word

visual.alt: Table comparing skimming and scanning: skimming finds the general idea by reading the title, opening, closing and first lines; scanning finds one detail by jumping to keywords, names and numbers.

slides.narration: Skimming and scanning are two kinds of fast reading. When you skim, your eyes move over the title, the opening, the closing and the first line of each paragraph, to catch the gist. When you scan, you hunt for one target, such as a name, a figure or the paragraph a question names. Use skimming for main idea questions and scanning for detail questions.

slides.heading: Check: the fastest route to the main idea
slides.narration: Your turn. You have thirty seconds to find out what a passage is mainly about. Which way of reading gets you there fastest?

slides.heading: How a discursive passage is built
slides.body_md: Most discursive passages follow the same shape. Spotting each part tells you where the answers are.

rows: hooks the reader with a scene, question or surprising fact
Ask any…, Imagine…, On a May afternoon…
Yet…, The truth is…, This matters because…
admits a limit or the other side
None of this means…, Of course…, However…
sums up or calls for action
So…, In short…, The next time you…

visual.alt: Table of the five parts of a discursive passage, what each does and the words that signal it: opening, claim, reasons and examples, counter-point and conclusion.

slides.narration: Most discursive passages share a shape. An opening hooks you with a scene or a question. A claim states the writer’s view, often with a word like yet. Reasons and examples support it. A counter-point admits a limit, with words like none of this means. And a conclusion sums up or calls for action. Learn the signal words and you will find answers faster.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: find the claim and its support
slides.body_md: *Many schools treat their gardens as decoration, a patch of marigolds by the gate. Yet a vegetable garden can be one of the best classrooms a school has. Students who grow spinach learn about soil, water and seasons far more vividly than from a diagram. They also learn patience, since nothing grows faster because you stare at it. And children who have grown a vegetable are often keener to eat it. A garden, in short, teaches science, character and healthy habits at once.*
bullets: **Opening:** gardens treated as decoration.
**Claim (topic sentence):** a vegetable garden can be one of the best classrooms (signalled by *Yet*).
**Three reasons:** science made vivid · patience · healthy eating (signalled by *also*, *And*).
**Conclusion:** *in short* sums up all three.
slides.narration: Look at this short SOYL paragraph. The opening sets up a common view: gardens as decoration. The word yet turns to the writer’s claim, that a vegetable garden is a great classroom. Then come three reasons, marked by also and and: science, patience and healthy eating. Finally, in short sums up all three. A main idea question here has one answer: the garden as a classroom.

slides.heading: Inference: reading between the lines
slides.body_md: An inference is a conclusion the writer **suggests but does not state**. Every inference must rest on a clue in the text.

rows: Her tiffin came back full for the third day.
a change in a daily habit
She had stopped humming as she got ready.
The new geometry box lay unopened.
she has lost interest in school work

visual.alt: Table showing inference: what the text says, what we can infer from it, and the clue that supports each inference.
visual.caption: Inference = text clue + reasoning. It is never a wild guess.

slides.narration: Inference means reading between the lines. The writer does not say it directly, but the clues point to it. In this example, a full tiffin box, a girl who has stopped humming and an unopened geometry box all suggest that something is troubling her at school. Notice that each inference rests on a clue. If you cannot point to a clue, it is a guess, not an inference.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an inference question
slides.body_md:
*Nisha's tiffin came back full for the third day running. Her mother noticed that she no longer hummed while getting ready, and that her new geometry box lay unopened on the desk.*

**Question:** What can Nisha's mother infer?
bullets: **Inference:** something at school is upsetting Nisha.
**Clue 1:** she has stopped eating her lunch.
**Clue 2:** a sign of her happiness (humming) has gone.
**Not acceptable:** she is ill, or she dislikes geometry: no clue supports these.
slides.narration: Here is how to answer an inference question. State the inference: something at school is upsetting Nisha. Then point to the clues: the uneaten lunch and the humming that has stopped. Notice the answers that are not acceptable. Saying she is ill, or that she hates geometry, goes beyond the clues. An inference must be the most reasonable reading of the evidence.

slides.heading: Check: make an inference
slides.narration: Try one. A boy checks his watch for the fifth time and stares down an empty road. What is the most reasonable inference?

slides.heading: Tone: the writer's attitude
slides.body_md: Tone is **how** the writer feels about the subject. Name it with a precise word and prove it with the writer's words.

rows: triumph, remarkable, worked through the night
failed, careless, at last… only after
those days, will never come back
if this continues, may have to

visual.alt: Table of seven tone words with their meanings and typical clues: admiring, critical, sarcastic, nostalgic, apprehensive, objective and balanced.

slides.narration: Tone is the writer’s attitude to the subject. It might be admiring, critical, sarcastic, nostalgic, worried, objective or balanced. You find it in word choice. Positive words like triumph show admiration. Saying the opposite of what is meant shows sarcasm. Figures and neutral verbs show an objective tone. In an exam, choose the most precise tone word, and back it with a phrase from the passage.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: three sentences, three tones
bullets: *At last the council has found money to mend the road, only eleven years after the first complaint.* — **sarcastic / critical** (*at last… only eleven years*)
*The volunteers worked through the night, and by dawn every family had a dry place to sleep.* — **admiring** (praise of effort and result)
*If the river keeps rising at this rate, the lower villages may have to be emptied by evening.* — **apprehensive** (*if… may have to*)
slides.narration: Here are three SOYL sentences. The first says at last and only eleven years: it pretends to praise but really criticises, so it is sarcastic. The second praises the volunteers’ effort and its result, so it is admiring. The third uses if and may have to, words of worry about the future, so it is apprehensive. In each case, the tone comes from a few telling words.

slides.heading: Check: name the tone
slides.narration: Your turn. A writer remembers summer evenings on a grandmother’s terrace, with jasmine and a distant radio, that will never come back. Which tone word fits best?

slides.heading: Vocabulary in context
slides.body_md: You do not need a dictionary. The sentence around an unfamiliar word nearly always contains a clue.

rows: the meaning is given beside the word
The herbivores, animals that eat only plants, …
a word of similar meaning is nearby
a word like unlike or but shows the opposite
Unlike her gregarious brother, she liked being alone
examples show what the word covers
citrus fruits such as lemons and oranges
the whole sentence points to the meaning
neither side would move: an impasse

visual.alt: Table of five context-clue types: definition, synonym, contrast, example and general sense, each with a SOYL example.

slides.narration: Vocabulary questions test whether you can use context. Look for five kinds of clue. A definition placed beside the word. A synonym nearby. A contrast word, such as unlike or but, that points to the opposite. Examples that show what the word covers. Or the general sense of the whole sentence. These clues work in every passage, on every topic.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: find the word, choose the meaning
slides.body_md: *The speaker's remarks were so candid that the audience gasped: she admitted every mistake her team had made.*
bullets: **Part of speech:** *candid* describes the remarks, so it is an adjective.
**Clue:** the colon explains it, since she admitted every mistake.
**Meaning:** frank, completely honest.
**Substitution test:** *so frank that the audience gasped* still makes sense.
**Find-the-word rule:** the answer must be the passage's own word, in the same part of speech as the meaning given.
slides.narration: Here is a four-step method. First, decide the part of speech: candid describes the remarks, so it is an adjective. Second, find the clue: after the colon, she admits every mistake. Third, state the meaning: frank and honest. Fourth, test it by putting your meaning in place of the word. For find-the-word questions, always give the passage’s own word, in the same form.

slides.heading: Check: use a contrast clue
slides.narration: Try this one. Unlike her gregarious brother, who loved parties, Anu preferred her own company. Use the contrast to work out the meaning of gregarious.

slides.heading: Answering 1-mark and 2-mark questions
bullets: **Multiple choice:** eliminate options the passage does not support; beware options that are true in life but not in the passage.
**Complete the sentence:** continue the given words grammatically.
**Two-mark answers:** point + evidence + explanation, about 30–40 words, in your own words.
**Evaluation (Do you agree…?):** either view, if it is supported.

visual.alt: Flow for a two-mark answer: a point that answers the question, evidence from the passage in your own words, and a short explanation.
visual.caption: About 30–40 words.

slides.narration: Now, how to write answers. For multiple choice, eliminate options the passage does not support, and beware options that are true in real life but not in the text. When completing a sentence, continue the words you are given grammatically. A two-mark answer needs a point, evidence and a short explanation, in about thirty to forty words. For do you agree questions, either view earns marks if you support it.

slides.heading: How the discursive passage is marked
slides.body_md: The board fixes the total (10 marks); SOYL models it with six 1-mark parts and two 2-mark parts. Accuracy and relevance earn marks, not length.

rows: a grammatical completion with the right idea
the correct choice, checked against the passage
the exact word from the named paragraph
a point plus support or a reasoned view

visual.alt: Table of the part types in a SOYL model of question one, with marks: multiple choice, complete the sentence, true or false and find the word earn one mark each; short answers of about thirty to forty words earn two marks each.
visual.caption: SOYL model of the board pattern: six 1-mark parts and two 2-mark parts = 10.

slides.narration: Here is how SOYL models the ten marks. Six one-mark parts: multiple choice on purpose, inference or tone, a sentence to complete, a true or false statement, and a word to find. Then two two-mark answers of about thirty to forty words. Marks reward the right point with support. Copying long chunks of the passage, or writing much more than needed, earns nothing extra.

slides.heading: Summary: the discursive passage
bullets: Five steps: questions → skim → scan → read closely → answer and check.
Know the shape: opening, claim, reasons, counter-point, conclusion.
Inference = clue + reasoning; tone = attitude shown by word choice.
Use context clues; give the passage's own word in the right form.
Two-mark answers: point + evidence + explanation, about 30–40 words.

visual.alt: Flow of the five-step reading plan: read the questions, skim for the gist, scan for each answer, read those lines closely, then answer and check.
visual.caption: SOYL five-step plan for any unseen passage.

slides.narration: To sum up. Follow the five steps: questions, skim, scan, read closely, answer and check. Know the shape of a discursive passage, so you can find the claim, reasons and counter-point. Base every inference on a clue, and name tone precisely. Use context clues for vocabulary, and give the passage’s own word. And keep two-mark answers to a point, evidence and explanation.

slides.heading: Exam tips: the discursive passage
bullets: Spend about 20–22 minutes on Q1; do not let it eat into the literature section.
Answer from the passage, not from general knowledge.
Watch for NOT and EXCEPT in questions.
For find-the-word questions, check the paragraph number and the part of speech.
Common slips: copying whole sentences; one-word answers to 2-mark questions; tone words that are too vague (*good*, *bad*).
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give the discursive passage about twenty minutes, then move on. Answer only from the passage, even when you know more about the topic. Watch for the words not and except in questions. In find the word questions, check the paragraph number and the part of speech. And avoid the usual slips: copying whole sentences, one-word answers to two-mark questions, and vague tone words like good.

decks.title: Unseen Passages — Part 2: The Case-Based Factual Passage
goals: Read tables and bar charts accurately, with their units
Link claims in a factual passage to the figures in its visual input
Use percentages, percentage points, fractions and multiples correctly
Draw fair conclusions and spot claims the figures do not support
Answer 1-mark and 2-mark questions on text and visual together

slides.heading: Unseen Passages — Part 2: The Case-Based Factual Passage
slides.body_md: Q2 of Section A is a **factual passage of 200–250 words with a visual input**, usually a table or chart, worth 10 marks. Questions use the text, the visual, or both together.

rows: Discursive passage: a writer discusses an issue, argues a view or weighs both sides
Case-based factual passage with visual input (table, chart or similar)

visual.alt: Table of the two Section A questions: question one, a discursive passage of four hundred to four hundred and fifty words for ten marks; question two, a case-based factual passage with a table or chart, two hundred to two hundred and fifty words, for ten marks.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section A: Reading Skills, 20 marks.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. The second passage in Section A is factual. It reports on something real-world, such as a survey, a scheme or a trend, in about two hundred to two hundred and fifty words, and it comes with a table or a chart. Some questions use only the text, some only the visual, and the hardest use both together.

slides.heading: Read the visual before the questions trip you
slides.body_md: Spend one minute on the visual: what it measures, in what unit, and where the big features are.

nodes.label: Match each claim to a figure

visual.alt: Flow for reading a visual input: title and caption, labels and units, highest, lowest and biggest change, what the text claims, and matching each claim to a figure.

slides.narration: Before you answer, spend one minute on the visual. Read its title and caption, so you know what is being measured, where and when. Read the labels and units. Find the highest value, the lowest, and the biggest change. Then read the text, and for each claim it makes, find the figure that matches. Many wrong answers come from skipping this minute.

slides.heading: Reading a table
slides.body_md: Read **across** a row to follow one item; read **down** a column to compare items at one time. Check the unit in each heading.

visual.alt: Table of a school planting drive: in 2022, 200 saplings planted and 120 alive after a year, a survival rate of 60 per cent; in 2023, 250 planted and 190 alive, 76 per cent; in 2024, 300 planted and 255 alive, 85 per cent.
visual.caption: A school's sapling drive (illustrative data)

slides.narration: Let us read a table. Each row here is a year of a school’s planting drive. Read across a row to follow one year: in twenty twenty-two, two hundred saplings were planted and one hundred and twenty survived, sixty per cent. Read down a column to compare years. The survival rate climbs from sixty to seventy-six to eighty-five per cent. That climb is the story of this table.

slides.heading: Reading a bar chart
slides.body_md: The **horizontal axis** shows the categories or time; the **vertical axis** shows the quantity and its unit. Compare bar heights only after checking the scale.

visual.alt: Bar chart of average daily steps in a Class 9 section during a six-week fitness challenge: 5,200 in week 1, 6,100 in week 2, 6,800 in week 3, 7,400 in week 4, 7,300 in week 5 and 8,100 in week 6.
visual.caption: Average daily steps, Class 9 fitness challenge (illustrative data)

slides.narration: Now a bar chart. Along the bottom are the six weeks of a fitness challenge. Up the side are average steps per day. Each bar’s height is the value for that week. The pattern is a steady rise, with one small dip in week five, from seven thousand four hundred to seven thousand three hundred. Small dips like this are exactly what examiners like to ask about.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: three questions on the chart
bullets: **Which week shows the only fall?** Week 5 (7,400 → 7,300).
**By how much did average steps rise from week 1 to week 6?** 8,100 − 5,200 = **2,900 steps**.
**Complete the sentence: The highest average was in week ___.** **6**, at 8,100 steps.
slides.narration: Here are three typical questions on that chart. Which week shows the only fall? Week five, from seven thousand four hundred to seven thousand three hundred. By how much did steps rise from week one to week six? Subtract: eight thousand one hundred minus five thousand two hundred is two thousand nine hundred steps. And the highest average? Week six. Always give the unit with your figure.

slides.heading: Check: what does the bar show?
slides.narration: Quick check. A chart has years along the bottom and rainfall in millimetres up the side. What does the height of each bar tell you?

slides.heading: The language of numbers
slides.body_md: Many marks are lost on wording, not arithmetic. A difference between two percentages is in **percentage points**.

rows: 40% → 30% is a fall of 10 percentage points
20 → 30 students is a 50 per cent increase

visual.alt: Table of number language for factual passages: percentage points, per cent, fractions, multiples, by for the size of change and to for the final value.

slides.narration: Number language matters. When two percentages differ, say percentage points: forty to thirty per cent is a fall of ten points. A change measured against the starting figure is a per cent change: twenty to thirty students is a fifty per cent rise. Use fractions like a quarter, and multiples like doubled. And remember: rose by gives the size of the change, rose to gives the final value.

slides.heading: Check: points or per cent?
slides.narration: Fill the blank. A chart shows a rise from twenty-five per cent to thirty-five per cent. What word completes the phrase ten percentage what?

slides.heading: Linking the text and the visual
bullets: The text often **summarises** the visual: check that its words match the figures.
The text gives **reasons**; the visual gives **sizes**. Two-mark answers often need both.
If the text says *more than double*, check: is the new figure more than twice the old?
If text and visual seem to disagree, trust the figures and say so.
slides.narration: The hardest questions link the text and the visual. Usually the text gives reasons and the visual gives sizes, so a good two-mark answer uses both: the cause from the passage and the figure from the chart. Check every summary word against the numbers. If the text says more than double, multiply the old figure by two and compare. If they disagree, trust the figures and say so.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: does the figure support the claim?
slides.body_md: *Demo text:* *By the end of the challenge, the class had nearly doubled its daily steps.*
bullets: **Ratio:** 8,100 ÷ 5,200 ≈ 1.6, about one and a half times.
**Verdict:** the claim overstates the rise. A fair summary: *daily steps rose by more than half, from 5,200 to 8,100.*
slides.narration: Suppose the text says the class nearly doubled its steps. Check it. Double five thousand two hundred is ten thousand four hundred, but week six is only eight thousand one hundred. That is about one and a half times, not nearly double. So the claim overstates the rise. A fair summary would say steps rose by more than half. Judging claims like this earns evaluation marks.

slides.heading: Five traps in factual passages

rows: thousand or lakh? hours or minutes? per cent or a number?
do not judge size by bar height alone
two things rising together do not prove a cause
is a 2-point rise really far more popular?
one class, one month or one survey proves little

visual.alt: Table of five traps in factual passages and what to check: units, axes that do not start at zero, mistaking things that happen together for cause, overclaiming words, and small samples or single periods.

slides.narration: Watch for five traps. Wrong units: thousands, lakhs, hours or minutes. Axes that do not start at zero, which make small differences look huge. Things that rise together, which do not prove that one causes the other. Overclaiming words, like far more popular for a tiny change. And small samples or a single period, which cannot prove a lasting trend. Naming a trap is often the key to a two-mark answer.

slides.heading: Check: together is not because
slides.narration: True or false? Ice cream sales and swimming accidents both rise in summer. Does that prove ice cream causes the accidents? Think about what else changes in summer.

slides.heading: Vocabulary in factual passages
bullets: Factual passages use **report words**: *respondents, survey, benchmark, decline, subsidy, restoration, seasonal*.
The meaning is usually clear from the sentence: *a government subsidy began to cover part of the cost*.
Find-the-word questions follow the same rule as Q1: the passage's own word, in the right form.
Phrasal verbs matter too: *pay off*, *catch up*, *level off*.
slides.narration: Factual passages use report words, such as respondents, benchmark, decline and subsidy. Their meaning is usually clear from the sentence. A subsidy that covers part of the cost must be money that lowers the price. Find the word questions follow the same rule as before: give the passage’s own word in the right form. Watch phrasal verbs too, like pay off and level off.

slides.heading: Check: express a proportion
slides.narration: One more. In a survey, two hundred out of eight hundred students read a newspaper daily. Which phrase describes that proportion most accurately?

slides.heading: How the factual passage is marked
slides.body_md: Accurate figures **with units** and a clear link between text and visual earn the marks. Opinions not supported by the passage do not.

rows: Read a value or rank from the visual
the exact figure with its unit
Complete a sentence with a figure or calculation
True / false using text and visual
the correct choice, checked against both
the exact word from the passage
Explain a trend or judge a claim (about 30–40 words)
a point plus accurate figures, or a supported view

visual.alt: Table of part types in a SOYL model of question two with marks: reading a value, completing with a figure, true or false and find the word earn one mark each; explaining a trend or judging a claim earns two marks.
visual.caption: SOYL model of the board pattern: six 1-mark parts and two 2-mark parts = 10.

slides.narration: Here is how SOYL models the ten marks of question two. Six one-mark parts: read a value, complete a sentence with a figure, decide true or false using both text and visual, and find a word. Then two two-mark answers: explain a trend with figures, or judge whether a claim is supported. Accurate figures, with units, are what turn a vague answer into a full-mark answer.

slides.heading: Summary: the case-based factual passage
bullets: One minute on the visual: title, units, highest, lowest, biggest change.
Rows across, columns down; check the scale before comparing bars.
Percentage points for gaps between percentages; check every multiple.
Text gives reasons, visual gives sizes: use both in 2-mark answers.
Watch the traps: units, axes, together-is-not-because, overclaiming, small samples.

nodes.label: Match each claim to a figure

visual.alt: Flow for reading a visual input: title and caption, labels and units, highest, lowest and biggest change, what the text claims, and matching each claim to a figure.

slides.narration: To sum up. Spend a minute on the visual first. Read tables across and down, and check the scale before comparing bars. Use percentage points for gaps between percentages, and check every claim of doubling or tripling. In two-mark answers, combine the reason from the text with the figure from the visual. And watch the five traps.

slides.heading: Exam tips: the factual passage
bullets: Spend about 15–18 minutes on Q2.
Always write units: *6.4 hours*, *11,000 trips*, *51 per cent*.
Show a quick calculation when you use one (*6,300 − 4,100 = 2,200*).
True/false items often need both the text and the visual.
Common slips: per cent for percentage points; reading the wrong row; adding reasons the passage never gives.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give the factual passage about fifteen to eighteen minutes. Always write the unit with every figure. If you calculate, show the quick working in one line. Remember that true or false items often need both the text and the visual. And watch the classic slips: per cent where you mean percentage points, reading the wrong row, and inventing reasons that the passage never gives.

notes.title: Reading Comprehension: Unseen Passages — Class 10 board notes

sections.heading: 1. Section A at a glance
sections.body_md:
Section A (Reading Skills, **20 marks**) has two unseen passages:

- **Q1 Discursive passage** (400–450 words, 10 marks): the writer discusses an issue or argues a view.
- **Q2 Case-based factual passage with visual input** (200–250 words, 10 marks): a report with a table, chart or similar visual.

Questions mix multiple choice, true/false, complete-the-sentence, find-the-word and short answers of about 30–40 words. Every passage is new to you, so the skills, not the topic, are what you prepare.

key_terms.definition_md: A passage you have not read before, set to test reading skills rather than knowledge.
Discussing an issue from a point of view, with reasons and often a counter-point.

rows: Discursive passage: a writer discusses an issue, argues a view or weighs both sides
Case-based factual passage with visual input (table, chart or similar)

visual.alt: Table of the two Section A questions: question one, a discursive passage of four hundred to four hundred and fifty words for ten marks; question two, a case-based factual passage with a table or chart, two hundred to two hundred and fifty words, for ten marks.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section A: Reading Skills, 20 marks.

sections.heading: 2. Reading strategies: skim, scan, read closely
sections.body_md:
**Five-step plan:** read the questions → skim for the gist → scan for each answer → read those lines closely → answer and check.

**Skimming** (for the general idea): title, first and last paragraphs, first sentence of each paragraph.

**Scanning** (for one detail): jump to keywords, names, numbers or the paragraph named in the question.

**Close reading** (for inference, tone and evaluation): read the sentence before and after the key line.

key_terms.definition_md: Reading quickly for the general idea of a passage.
Searching quickly for one specific detail.
The general meaning or main idea.

visual.alt: Flow of the five-step reading plan: read the questions, skim for the gist, scan for each answer, read those lines closely, then answer and check.
visual.caption: SOYL five-step plan for any unseen passage.

rows: title, first and last paragraphs, first line of each paragraph
very fast, jumping to the target
who, when, how many, which word

visuals.alt: Table comparing skimming and scanning: skimming finds the general idea by reading the title, opening, closing and first lines; scanning finds one detail by jumping to keywords, names and numbers.

sections.heading: 3. The shape of an argument
sections.body_md:
Most discursive passages follow this shape: **opening** (a hook) → **claim** (the writer's view) → **reasons and examples** → **counter-point** (a limit or the other side) → **conclusion** (summary or call to action).

Signal words help: *Yet, The truth is* (claim); *First, Also, For example* (reasons); *None of this means, Of course, However* (counter-point); *So, In short* (conclusion).

**Main idea questions** need an answer that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph. **Writer's purpose questions** ask why a detail is there (to hook, to prove, to contrast, to persuade).

sections.heading: 4. Inference and evaluation
sections.body_md:
**Inference** is a conclusion the text suggests but does not state. It must rest on a clue: *a full tiffin box, no humming, an unopened geometry box → something is troubling her*. Reject options that go beyond the clues.

**Evaluation** asks you to judge: *Do you agree? Is the claim convincing? Which suggestion is most practical?* Either view earns marks if it is supported by the passage.

**Fact or opinion:** a fact can be checked (*attendance rose from 88 to 94 per cent*); an opinion judges or recommends (*every school should…*).

sections.heading: 5. Tone and attitude
sections.body_md:
Tone is the writer's attitude, shown through word choice. Useful tone words: **admiring, appreciative, critical, sarcastic, ironic, nostalgic, apprehensive, concerned, objective, balanced, optimistic, pessimistic, humorous**.

Prove a tone with the writer's words: *How wonderful that cars can now reach the next traffic jam sooner* is sarcastic because it praises something bad. A paragraph that admits *None of this means structure is the enemy* is balanced.

Avoid vague words such as *good*, *bad* or *nice*.

sections.heading: 6. Vocabulary in context
sections.body_md:
**Five clue types:** definition, synonym, contrast, example, general sense.

**Method:** (1) decide the part of speech; (2) find the clue; (3) state the meaning; (4) test it by substitution.

**Find-the-word questions:** give the passage's own word, from the paragraph named, in the same part of speech as the meaning given (*unpleasant to bear* → *uncomfortable*, an adjective). A synonym of your own does not earn the mark.

sections.heading: 7. The case-based factual passage and its visual
sections.body_md:
**Read the visual first:** title and caption, labels and units, highest, lowest, biggest change. Then match each claim in the text to a figure.

**Tables:** read across a row to follow one item, down a column to compare. **Bar charts:** the horizontal axis gives categories or time; the vertical axis gives the quantity and unit; check where the scale starts.

**Number language:** percentage points for the gap between two percentages; per cent for change relative to the start; fractions (*a quarter*); multiples (*doubled*, *more than ten times*); *by* for the size of change, *to* for the final value.

**Traps:** wrong units; axes not starting at zero; things that happen together are not proof of cause; overclaiming words; small samples or a single period.

questions.passage_md:
1. Ask a group of Class 10 students how they spent last Sunday and you are likely to hear a timetable: tuition in the morning, a coaching test after lunch, an hour of revision, and whatever was left over handed to a phone. Very few will say that they did nothing at all. Fewer still will say it without a trace of guilt.

2. We have come to treat empty time as wasted time. Parents worry that an idle child is falling behind; schools fill the holidays with projects; and teenagers themselves reach for a screen the moment a conversation pauses or a bus is late. The result is a generation that is rarely bored, but also rarely alone with its own thoughts.

3. That loss matters more than it seems. Boredom is uncomfortable precisely because it pushes the mind to look for something to do, and when no ready-made entertainment is available, the mind starts to make its own. A child staring out of a train window begins to invent stories about the people on the platform. A student with no plan for the afternoon may finally pick up the guitar gathering dust in the corner. Many people who are good at solving problems say that their best ideas came not at the desk but on a walk, in the shower or while waiting for something else.

4. Unstructured time also teaches a quieter skill: the ability to manage one's own attention. When every minute is scheduled by someone else, a young person learns to follow instructions efficiently. When an afternoon is truly free, the same person has to decide what is worth doing, notice when interest fades, and choose again. These are the habits of an independent adult, and they cannot be learnt from a timetable.

5. None of this means that structure is the enemy. Practice, coaching and revision are essential, especially in a board year, and a completely aimless routine would be as unhealthy as a crowded one. The argument is about balance. A schedule with no gaps leaves no room for the mind to wander, and wandering, it turns out, is where a great deal of thinking happens.

6. So the next time you find yourself with half an hour and nothing to fill it, resist the urge to reach for your phone. Sit with the boredom for a while. Look out of the window, doodle in the margin of a notebook, or simply let your thoughts drift. You may be surprised by where they take you.

questions.passage_md:
1. In almost every Indian town there is a narrow shop, often no wider than a cupboard, where a man with a magnifying glass brings dead things back to life. Watches, mixers, radios, phones and pressure cookers arrive in plastic bags and leave working again, usually for less than the price of a cinema ticket. For generations this was simply how households treated their belongings: when something broke, you mended it.

2. That habit is fading. Many modern gadgets are sealed shut with glue rather than screws, spare parts are hard to find, and a new model is advertised before the old one has been paid for. Faced with a cracked screen or a dead battery, buyers are often told that a repair will cost almost as much as a replacement. Some makers even warn that opening a device yourself will cancel its guarantee. So they shrug and buy new.

3. The cost of that shrug does not appear on any bill. Every discarded device carries metals that were mined, refined and shipped across the world, and much of that material ends up in landfills or in informal recycling yards where workers, sometimes children, burn wires to recover copper. Electronic waste is among the fastest-growing kinds of rubbish on the planet, and most of it is never properly recycled.

4. Repair offers a simple way to slow this flow. A phone that lasts five years instead of two sharply reduces how many new phones a household buys. Repair also keeps money and skills within the local economy. The person who fixes your fan is a neighbour, not a distant factory, and the knowledge in his hands was often passed down from a parent or an older master.

5. In several countries, campaigners have begun to argue for a right to repair: manufacturers, they say, should sell spare parts, publish repair manuals and design products that can be opened with ordinary tools. Some governments have started to listen. Meanwhile, volunteers in many cities run repair cafés, where people bring broken items and learn to fix them alongside experienced helpers.

6. Young people can play a part too. Before replacing something, ask whether it can be repaired, and if the answer is no, ask why. Learn to change a fuse, sew on a button or fit a bicycle chain; most of these skills can be picked up in an afternoon from a parent, a neighbour or the repair shop down the road. These small acts may not feel heroic, but each repaired object is one less item in a landfill and one more skill kept alive.

questions.passage_md:
1. A girl growing up in Bengaluru might speak Kannada with the vegetable seller, Tamil with her grandmother, Hindi with her friends from the next building and English in the classroom, all before dinner. Visitors from countries where most people speak a single language are often astonished by this. In India, it is simply an ordinary day.

2. Yet many families quietly treat this richness as a problem to be solved. Parents who want their children to succeed sometimes stop speaking their home language at the dinner table, worried that it will slow down the child's English. Within a generation, a language that the grandparents spoke fluently may survive only in a few songs and a handful of kitchen words. Children grow up able to understand their grandparents but not to answer them, and talk across the generations shrinks to smiles and nods.

3. The worry is understandable but largely mistaken. Researchers who study bilingual children have found that learning two or more languages does not confuse young minds; if anything, it seems to train them. A child who keeps switching between languages must track who understands what, and must hold back one set of words while using another. Many studies suggest that this practice helps attention and flexible thinking, although scientists still debate how large and lasting the benefits are.

4. Other gains are easier to see. A person who speaks the language of a neighbourhood is trusted there in a way an outsider is not. A doctor who can explain an illness in a patient's own language is more likely to be understood and followed. A writer who moves between two languages can borrow images and sayings from each, enriching both. Businesses, too, value staff who can speak to customers in more than one language.

5. Languages also carry memory. Proverbs, lullabies, recipes and the names people give to hills, rivers and plants often exist in only one tongue. When that tongue disappears, the knowledge it held does not simply move into English or Hindi; much of it is lost. Language experts warn that a large share of the world's roughly seven thousand languages could stop being spoken within this century.

6. Learning English well and keeping a home language alive are not rival goals. Schools can value the languages children bring with them, and families can keep at least one meal a day in the language of the grandparents. Even a few songs, stories and games in the home language can carry it into the next generation. A country that speaks in many voices has nothing to apologise for. It has a treasure to protect.

questions.passage_md:
1. Walk into any school assembly in the week after results and you will hear the names of toppers read out to applause. Nobody reads out the names of those who tried something difficult and fell short. This is natural, but it teaches a lopsided lesson: that success is the only story worth telling.

2. Look closely at almost any achievement and you will find a long trail of failure behind it. A batter who scores a century has been dismissed cheaply many more times than the crowd remembers. A scientist who announces a discovery has usually spent years on experiments that went nowhere. Space agencies, India's among them, have lost rockets and spacecraft on the way to their goals, and have treated each loss as a lesson rather than a disgrace.

3. Failure is useful because it gives information that success cannot. When a plan works, we rarely ask why; we simply repeat it. When it fails, we are forced to look for the weak link. A student who studies a poor test paper question by question learns far more than one who glances at the total and hides the paper in a drawer. Many top athletes watch recordings of their own defeats for exactly this reason.

4. The difficulty is that failure hurts, and the hurt is often made worse by the people around us. A child who is laughed at for a wrong answer learns to stop raising her hand. A teenager who is compared unfavourably with a cousin learns that it is safer not to try than to try and fall short. Over time, such children choose easy tasks they are sure to finish rather than hard ones that might stretch them. Fear of failure, rather than failure itself, is what most often stops young people from growing.

5. Schools and families can change this. Teachers can praise a thoughtful mistake as well as a correct answer. Parents can share stories of their own setbacks instead of presenting themselves as people who never stumbled. Students can keep a mistakes notebook in which every error is written down along with what it taught them. A school could even hold an assembly at which students and teachers each describe a failure and what they learnt from it.

6. None of this means celebrating carelessness. A failure that comes from not preparing teaches very little except the obvious. The failures worth honouring are those that come from attempting something hard. If we want young people to attempt hard things, we must stop treating every stumble as a disaster and start treating it as part of the climb.

questions.passage_md:
1. On a May afternoon in most Indian cities, the difference between a street lined with trees and a bare one is not a matter of opinion. You can feel it on your skin. Step out of the shade of a large neem or peepal onto open tar and the heat rises from the ground like the breath of an oven. Even birds and stray dogs know this, crowding under the few trees that remain.

2. Trees cool a city in two ways. Their leaves block sunlight before it reaches roads, walls and roofs, which would otherwise soak up the heat and give it out slowly through the night. Trees also draw water from the soil and release it as vapour through their leaves, a process that takes heat from the surrounding air, much as sweat cools the body. A street under a full canopy can be several degrees cooler than one without.

3. Yet trees are often the first casualties of growth. Roads are widened, footpaths are paved right up to the trunk, and old trees are cut to make room for flyovers and parking. Replacement saplings are planted in neat rows for photographs and then forgotten. Many die in their first summer for want of water and protection. And a sapling is no substitute for a lost giant: it takes decades to grow a canopy wide enough to shade a street.

4. The choice of tree matters as much as the number. Some ornamental species brought from other continents look attractive in a brochure but give little shade, need more water and offer nothing to local birds and insects. Native trees such as neem, jamun, banyan and arjun have grown up with the local climate. Once established, they survive dry spells and support a web of life, from bees to barbets.

5. Shade is also a question of fairness. Wealthier neighbourhoods tend to have parks and tree-lined avenues, while crowded settlements, where people can least afford air-conditioning, are often the hottest and barest. Planting trees there is not decoration. It is a public health measure that can reduce heat stress during long summers, when children, older people and outdoor workers such as street vendors suffer most.

6. Citizens need not wait for the municipality. Housing societies can adopt a stretch of road; schools can plant native saplings and give students the duty of watering them through their first two summers; and anyone can object when a healthy old tree is marked for cutting. A tree planted today will not cool your street this year. But it may cool someone's street for the next hundred years.

questions.passage_md:
1. When almost any fact can be found in seconds on a phone, it is fair to ask why towns still need public libraries. The question is not new. People asked it when radio arrived, and again when television did. Each time, libraries were expected to fade. Each time, they changed and survived.

2. The first answer is that a library was never only a store of facts. A search engine is excellent at answering a question you already know how to ask. A library, especially its open shelves, is good at showing you questions you did not know existed. A student looking for a book on volcanoes may walk out with one on deep-sea creatures from the shelf beside it, and with a new interest. Browsing, the slow wandering along shelves without a fixed goal, is one of the oldest ways of learning, and one that a search box rarely allows.

3. The second answer is that information online is plentiful but uneven. Some of it is careful and accurate; much of it is careless, out of date or written to sell something. Librarians are trained to tell the difference, and a good one can teach a young reader how to judge a source, a skill that matters more, not less, in a world flooded with information.

4. Third, a library is one of the few indoor public spaces where nobody expects you to buy anything. In a crowded city it offers a quiet table, a fan, clean water and light to study by; in summer it is often one of the coolest rooms in the neighbourhood. For a student who shares a single room with a large family, that table can make the difference between passing and failing an examination.

5. Libraries around the world have adapted to these needs. Many now lend laptops, run coding clubs, hold story hours for toddlers and help older people learn to use online services. In several Indian states, small community libraries run by volunteers have opened in villages, giving children their first chance to hold a storybook that is not a textbook. Some libraries send small vans of books to areas that have no library building at all.

6. None of this happens by itself. Libraries need funding, trained staff and, above all, readers. The surest way to keep a library alive is to use it: to borrow a book, attend a reading, or simply sit and study there. A town that lets its library close does not only lose a building. It loses one of the few places where curiosity is free.

questions.passage_md:
A survey of 1,200 students in six schools of Lucknow asked a simple question: how many hours do you usually sleep on a school night? The results, shown in the bar chart, suggest that sleep shrinks steadily as students move to higher classes.

Students in Class 6 reported close to nine hours a night. By Class 9 the figure had fallen below eight, and in the board year, Class 10, it dropped to just under seven. Class 12 students slept the least of all. Health experts generally advise that teenagers need about eight to ten hours of sleep for growth, memory and mood, so most senior students in the survey fall well short.

Asked what kept them awake, students most often named late tuition classes, homework and phones. Nearly half of the Class 10 respondents admitted using a phone in bed after the lights were off. Several said they slept longer on Sundays to catch up, although doctors point out that one long sleep at the weekend cannot fully repair a week of short nights.

The survey team suggests a few small changes: a fixed bedtime, keeping phones out of the bedroom, and switching off screens an hour before sleep. They also urge schools not to schedule extra classes very early in the morning.

Waste water from home purifiers, usually poured down the drain, can be collected to mop floors or water plants. The volunteers say they are not asking anyone to suffer, only to notice. questions.passage_md:
Every winter, birds from Central Asia, Siberia and the Himalaya fly thousands of kilometres to spend the cold months on the lakes and marshes of India. Bird watchers at one wetland in central India have counted these visitors on the same January weekend every year since 2019. Their counts are shown in the bar chart.

For the first two years the numbers were healthy, peaking at about 15,100 birds in 2020. Then came a worrying decline. New housing colonies were built along the northern shore, sewage began to flow into the lake, and a thick mat of water hyacinth spread across the open water where ducks once fed. By 2023 the count had fallen to 9,800, the lowest in the record.

That year, the forest department and local volunteers began a restoration programme. They removed most of the hyacinth, built a small plant to treat sewage before it reached the lake, and marked a quiet zone where boats were not allowed in winter. The birds responded quickly. The count rose in 2024 and climbed to 12,900 in 2025.

The bird watchers are cautiously hopeful. The numbers have not yet returned to their earlier level, and one good year can be followed by a bad one. Still, the recovery suggests that a damaged wetland can heal once the causes of the damage are removed.

The Young Explorers Online Science Fair began in 2023 with a simple idea: any student aged 12 to 17, anywhere in the world, could upload a short video of a science project and receive comments from volunteer scientists. questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** nostalgic. Fond memories of a past that is gone, with sensory details, create a nostalgic tone.

questions.stem_md: Read: *The bridge is 1.2 kilometres long and was opened to traffic in March.* The tone of this sentence is…
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** objective. It states checkable facts without any feeling or judgement.

questions.stem_md: Read: *The talks reached an impasse; neither side would move an inch.* What does *impasse* mean here?

options.text_md: a situation in which no progress is possible

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a situation in which no progress is possible. The clue after the semicolon (neither side would move) explains the word.

questions.stem_md: Read: *Unlike her gregarious brother, who loved parties, Anu preferred her own company.* What does *gregarious* mean?

options.text_md: fond of the company of others

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** fond of the company of others. The contrast word *Unlike* and the clue *who loved parties* show the meaning.

questions.stem_md: Read: *The herbivores, animals that eat only plants, gathered near the river.* Which kind of context clue explains *herbivores*?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a definition clue. The phrase between the commas defines the word directly.

questions.stem_md: Read: *Many villages in Rajasthan have repaired old earthen ponds called johads. Rainwater collected in them soaks into the ground and raises the water table. Wells that had been dry for years now hold water again.* Which is the best title for this paragraph?

options.text_md: Reviving a Traditional Way to Save Rainwater

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Reviving a Traditional Way to Save Rainwater. The title must cover the whole paragraph: the old ponds, how they work and the result.

questions.stem_md: A chart in a factual passage shows that the share of students who walk to school fell from 40 per cent to 30 per cent. Which statement is accurate?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It fell by 10 percentage points. The gap between two percentages is in percentage points: 40 − 30 = 10 points (a 25 per cent fall in the share).

questions.stem_md: A bar chart with a factual passage has years along the bottom and *Rainfall (mm)* on the side. What does the height of each bar show?

options.text_md: the number of rainy days in that year
the rainfall in millimetres in that year
the year with the most rain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the rainfall in millimetres in that year. The vertical axis label names what the bar height measures, with its unit.

questions.stem_md: A survey in a factual passage says that 200 of 800 students read a newspaper daily. Which phrase describes this most accurately?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a quarter of the students. 200 ÷ 800 = 1/4, a quarter.

questions.stem_md: Which question on an unseen passage tests **evaluation** rather than recall?

options.text_md: In which year did the survey take place?
Do you agree with the writer's view? Give a reason.
Who is the writer of the passage?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Do you agree with the writer's view? Give a reason. Evaluation asks you to judge the writer's ideas and support your judgement.

questions.stem_md: An unseen-passage question asks which option is NOT mentioned in the passage. What is the safest method?

options.text_md: Choose the option you personally disagree with.
Choose the first option that sounds unfamiliar.
Check each option against the passage and choose the one you cannot find.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Check each option against the passage and choose the one you cannot find. Eliminate the options that the passage does state; the one left is the answer.

questions.stem_md: A Section A question says *Complete the sentence appropriately.* What should your answer do?

options.text_md: Continue the given words grammatically, using the idea from the passage.
Copy a whole paragraph from the passage.
Give your own opinion of the topic.
Write one word only, whatever the sentence needs.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Continue the given words grammatically, using the idea from the passage. The completion must fit the given start and carry the right information.

questions.stem_md: Reading quickly for the general idea of a passage is called ___, while searching quickly for one specific detail is called ___.
questions.solution_md: General idea: **skimming**. Specific detail: **scanning**.

questions.stem_md: In the sentence *The tiny, almost minuscule, print was hard to read*, the word that helps you guess the meaning of *minuscule* is ___.
questions.solution_md: *Minuscule* is placed beside **tiny**, a synonym clue.

questions.stem_md: If a chart shows a rise from 25 per cent to 35 per cent, the rise is 10 percentage ___.
questions.solution_md: The gap between two percentages is measured in percentage **points**.

questions.stem_md: If the number of visitors to a fair went from 3,000 to 6,000, we can say the number ___.
questions.solution_md: 6,000 is twice 3,000, so it **doubled**.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the tone of a passage is the writer's attitude to the subject, shown mainly through word choice.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Tone is attitude; adjectives, adverbs and images reveal it.

questions.stem_md: True or false: *Pune is the best city in India for students* is a statement of fact.
questions.solution_md: **False.** It is an opinion: *best* is a judgement that cannot be checked.

questions.stem_md: True or false: when a question says *Find a word from the passage that means…*, any synonym from your own vocabulary will earn the mark.
questions.solution_md: **False.** The word must come from the passage (and usually from the paragraph named).

questions.stem_md: True or false: if a factual passage shows that ice-cream sales and swimming accidents both rise in summer, it proves that ice cream causes swimming accidents.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Two things rising together (often because of a third factor, hot weather) does not prove that one causes the other.

questions.stem_md: True or false: a 2-mark answer on an unseen passage should usually be about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Short answers in Section A are meant to be brief: one point with support, in roughly 30–40 words.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Reading the first and last paragraphs of a discursive passage often reveals its main idea quickly.

**Reason (R):** Writers commonly state their main point in the introduction and return to it in the conclusion.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the habit described in R is exactly why the method in A works.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a *find the word* question, the answer should be the same part of speech as the meaning given.

**Reason (R):** Examiners accept any word of similar meaning, even if it does not appear in the passage.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: a meaning given as an adjective needs an adjective. R is false: the word must come from the passage.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bar that is twice as tall as another always shows a value exactly twice as large, whatever the scale.

**Reason (R):** Before comparing bars, a reader should check where the vertical axis starts and what units it uses.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: if the axis does not start at zero, heights mislead. R is true, and it is the reason A fails.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In *He merely smiled when we gave him the prize*, the word *merely* suggests that the writer expected a stronger reaction.

**Reason (R):** A single passage can contain more than one tone.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R is a general point about passages and does not explain the effect of *merely* in A.

questions.stem_md: Match each reading strategy used in Section A with what it is best for.

match_right.text_md: finding a specific name, date or figure
getting the general idea of a passage

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Choose the strategy by the job: gist, detail, interpretation or meaning.

questions.stem_md: Match each tone word used in unseen-passage questions with its meaning.

match_right.text_md: mocking by saying the opposite of what is meant
factual and free of personal feeling

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Learn tone words in sets so that you can name an attitude precisely.

questions.stem_md: Match each Section A question with the skill it tests.

options.text_md: Why does the writer mention the space agencies?
In which year was the count highest?
What can you tell about the narrator's mood?

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Naming the skill tells you how to answer: find, explain, read off or infer.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps for tackling a discursive unseen passage in the order SOYL recommends.

options.text_md: Skim the passage for its main idea.
Check word limits, spelling and that every part is answered.
Write the answers in the order of the questions.
Find each answer and read the lines around it closely.
Read the questions to know what to look for.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (b). Questions first, then gist, then detail, then writing, then checking.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps for reading the visual input of a case-based factual passage.

options.text_md: Find the highest and lowest values.
Link what you found to the claims in the text.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (d) → (b) → (a) → (e). From what the visual is about, to how it is measured, to its key features, to the text.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between skimming and scanning an unseen passage, with one example of when you would use each. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: Define both + one use of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, for example to choose a title. Scanning means searching quickly for one detail, such as a date or figure asked for in a question.

questions.stem_md: Read: *The fridge held nothing but a single lemon, and the calendar on the wall still showed last month.* What can you infer about the people who live there? Give two clues. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: A sensible inference + two clues from the sentence.

answer.model_answer_md: They have probably been away, or too busy to look after the home. The almost empty fridge suggests nobody has shopped recently, and the calendar still on last month shows that nobody has turned the page.

questions.stem_md: Read: *Another urgent meeting, another hour of slides that nobody will remember.* Name the tone and justify it. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: A tone word + evidence from the wording (repetition, contrast).

answer.model_answer_md: The tone is weary and mildly sarcastic. Repeating the word another shows boredom with something that keeps happening, and calling the meeting urgent while saying nobody will remember it mocks its importance.

marking_scheme.step: Justified with words from the sentence

questions.stem_md: How can you work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word in an unseen passage without a dictionary? Give two strategies. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: Two strategies (context clue, substitution, word parts, part of speech).

answer.model_answer_md: First, look for a clue in the nearby words, such as a definition, a synonym or a contrast. Second, try putting a simpler word in its place and check whether the sentence still makes sense.

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between a fact and an opinion, using an example from a report on a school cricket match. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: Definitions + one example of each in a cricket context.

answer.model_answer_md: A fact can be checked, for example that the team won by twenty runs. An opinion is a personal judgement that others may dispute, such as calling the captain's innings the finest of the season.

questions.stem_md: A factual passage claims that *cycling to school has become far more popular*, but its table shows the share of students cycling rising from 12 per cent to 14 per cent. Does the table support the claim? Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: A judgement + the size of the change in points + why the wording overstates it.

answer.model_answer_md: Only weakly. Cycling did rise, but by just two percentage points, from 12 to 14 per cent. Calling that far more popular exaggerates a small change, so the claim overstates what the table shows.

marking_scheme.step: Supported by a reason or detail from the passage

questions.stem_md: Explain why a rise from 20 per cent to 30 per cent should not be called a 10 per cent increase. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: Percentage points (30 − 20 = 10) versus percentage change (10 ÷ 20 = 50 per cent).

answer.model_answer_md: The gap between the two shares is 10 percentage points. As a proportion of the starting figure, though, the rise is 10 out of 20, which is an increase of 50 per cent, not 10 per cent.

marking_scheme.step: Shows the 50 per cent relative increase

questions.stem_md: Read: *Many hill towns now ban plastic bags. Shops offer paper or cloth bags instead, and visitors are fined for littering. As a result, streams that were once choked with waste are running clear again.* State the main idea in one sentence and give one supporting detail. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: One-sentence main idea + one detail that supports it.

answer.model_answer_md: The main idea is that banning plastic bags has helped hill towns become cleaner. One supporting detail is that streams once blocked with waste now run clear, because shops use paper or cloth bags.

questions.stem_md: A discursive passage on screen time begins: *How many hours did you spend on your phone yesterday? Be honest.* Why might the writer open with a question? Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: Purpose of a rhetorical opening: engage the reader + make it personal.

answer.model_answer_md: The question pulls the reader in at once and makes the topic personal. Each reader starts counting their own hours, so they are already thinking about the problem before the writer begins to argue.

questions.stem_md: In a survey of 100 students, 70 wanted longer library hours, 20 did not mind and 10 wanted shorter hours. Write a conclusion that a writer could fairly draw from these figures. Answer in about 30–40 words.
questions.solution_md: A conclusion that stays within the figures (majority, 70 per cent) and avoids overclaiming (it is one survey of 100).

answer.model_answer_md: A clear majority of the students surveyed, seven in ten, would like longer library hours, while only one in ten wants them shorter. The school has good reason to consider extending the hours.

marking_scheme.step: Supported by a reason or detail from the passage
